Satan and the rebellious angels were created holy and good, but they were created morally mutable, meaning they possessed the genuine capacity to choose either obedience or rebellion. Sin did not originate from God or from heaven as a location, but arose within the heart of the creature through proud self-exaltation against the Creator.

When God completed His creation, everything was "very good" (Genesis 1:31). The angelic hosts lived in the presence of God in unblemished innocence. However, initial innocence is not the same as confirmed, unchangeable righteousness. Angels, like the first human beings in Eden, were created with creaturely freedom and moral responsibility. They had the ability not to sin, yet also the capacity to fall.

Scripture points to pride as the root of this initial rebellion. In warning against appointing a new convert as an overseer, Scripture mentions falling into "the same condemnation as the devil" through conceit (1 Timothy 3:6). Satan was not satisfied to be a creature serving God; he desired the glory, autonomy, and worship that belong to God alone. Reflecting on this rebellion, Scripture notes that the fallen angels "did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling" (Jude 1:6; 2 Peter 2:4). 

Theologically, evil is not an independent physical substance created by God, but a corruption and privation of the good. God is entirely light and in Him is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5), and He is never the author or instigator of sin (James 1:13). Evil arose when a creature turned its affection and will away from the supreme goodness of God toward itself. 

While heaven was entirely free from sin, it was not an environment that mechanically forced creatures to love God. Love and obedience required the creature's faithful allegiance. The moment Satan and his followers rebelled, sin was instantly judged, and they were cast out of God's favorable presence (Luke 10:18). 

For believers today, this truth serves as a sobering reminder of the destructive nature of pride (Proverbs 16:18), while also pointing us to the comfort of the Gospel. Whereas Satan sought to elevate himself and fell, Jesus Christ, who is God by nature, humbled Himself to take on human flesh, dying on the cross to destroy the works of the devil and redeem lost sinners (Philippians 2:5-8; 1 John 3:8). Those who are united to Christ by faith look forward to an eternal home where our righteousness will be permanently sealed, and sin will never rise again (Revelation 21:3-4).

question: What is the greatest sin?
answer:
From the perspective of Scripture, the greatest sin can be understood in two interrelated ways: the violation of the greatest commandment and the final, hardened rejection of God’s grace in Jesus Christ.

When Jesus was asked to name the greatest commandment in the Law, He answered, "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the first and greatest commandment" (Matthew 22:37-38). Consequently, the greatest sin is the refusal to love, honor, and obey the holy God who created us, choosing instead to enthrone ourselves or created things in His rightful place (Romans 1:21-25). James 2:10 reminds us that "whoever keeps the whole law and yet stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it." In that sense, every sin is an act of cosmic treason against our sovereign Creator.

In an ultimate and eternal sense, Jesus also spoke of a specific sin that will not be forgiven: the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Matthew 12:31-32; Mark 3:28-30). In its historical context, Jesus gave this warning to religious leaders who witnessed His miraculous works done by the Spirit of God and yet attributed them to Satan. This represents a deliberate, settled, and decisive hardening of the heart against the Holy Spirit’s testimony concerning Jesus. Because salvation is found only in Christ (Acts 4:12; John 14:6), the persistent, unrepentant rejection of the Holy Spirit’s call to trust in Jesus leaves a person outside the only means of mercy (Hebrews 10:26-29).

Yet the glorious message of the Gospel is that no past sin is beyond the reach of Christ's cleansing blood for the one who turns to Him in genuine faith. We all have broken God's law and stand guilty, unable to save ourselves by our own works (Romans 3:10-12; Romans 3:23). But in His great love and mercy, God sent His eternal Son, Jesus Christ, who took on human nature, lived a sinless life, and offered Himself on the cross as a penal substitutionary sacrifice to pay the penalty for our sins. He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily from the dead, triumphing over sin and death and ascending as Lord of all (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

Because of Christ's finished work, God freely offers justification and eternal life to all who believe (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:8-9). As the Apostle John writes, "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). 

Turn (repent) from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. 

What has prompted your thinking about this question today?

question: What does the Bible say about sedition?
answer:
The Bible addresses sedition, understood both as inciting unlawful rebellion against civil government and stirring up factious division within the church, as a sin that opposes God's design for order and peace. Scripture consistently calls believers to live quiet, submissive, and godly lives under God's sovereign authority.

### 1. Sedition as a Work of the Flesh
In the New Testament, the Greek word *dichostasia* (often translated as "dissensions," "divisions," or "seditions") refers to creating factions or stirring up rebellion. In Galatians 5:19–21, Paul explicitly names this among the works of the flesh:

> "Now the deeds of the flesh are evident, which are: immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, disputes, dissensions (*dichostasiai*), factions... those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God." (Galatians 5:19–21)

Another Greek term, *stasis*, refers directly to political rebellion, violent insurrection, or rioting against civil order. Scripture uses this term when describing Barabbas, who was imprisoned for murder and insurrection in the city (Luke 23:19; Mark 15:7). Paul was also falsely accused by his opponents of stirring up sedition among the Jews throughout the world (Acts 24:5).

### 2. Submission to Civil Authorities
God is the ultimate source of all earthly authority, having established human government as a minister of common grace to restrain evil and maintain public order (Romans 13:1–4). Because of this, rebellion against lawful civil governance is viewed as resistance against God's appointed order:

*   **Honoring Authorities:** "Every person is to be in subjection to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those which exist are established by God. Therefore whoever resists authority has opposed the ordinance of God; and they who have opposed will receive condemnation upon themselves." (Romans 13:1–2)
*   **Living as Free Servants of God:** "Submit yourselves for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether to a king as the one in authority, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of those who do right." (1 Peter 2:13–14)
*   **Praying for Rulers:** Believers are commanded to pray for kings and all who are in high positions, "so that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and dignity" (1 Timothy 2:1–2; Titus 3:1).

### 3. The Biblical Limit: Obeying God Rather Than Man
Scripture draws a vital distinction between lawless sedition and faithful obedience to God. When a governing authority demands that believers disobey God's moral law or forbids the proclamation of the Gospel, the Christian's ultimate allegiance belongs to Jesus Christ as Lord.

When the Jewish council ordered Peter and John to stop preaching the name of Jesus, the apostles responded: "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29; Acts 4:19–20). Similarly, the Hebrew midwives refused Pharaoh's command to kill infant boys (Exodus 1:17), and Daniel continued to pray despite the king's decree (Daniel 6:10). 

Even in these moments of necessary civil disobedience, God's people did not organize violent insurrections or stir up chaotic rebellion; instead, they willingly endured suffering and imprisonment, entrusting their souls to a faithful Creator (1 Peter 4:19).

### 4. Sedition and Division in the Church
The biblical principle against sedition applies just as strongly to the spiritual community. God despises the sowing of discord among brothers:

*   "There are six things which the Lord hates, yes, seven which are an abomination to Him... one who spreads strife among brothers." (Proverbs 6:16, 19)
*   "Now I urge you, brethren, keep your eye on those who cause dissensions and hindrances contrary to the teaching which you learned, and turn away from them." (Romans 16:17)

### Pastoral Application
For the Christian, overcoming the spirit of sedition begins in the heart. Rather than giving in to the anger, strife, and factionalism of this fallen world, believers are called to walk in progressive sanctification by the Holy Spirit. 

A practical step is to examine your speech and media habits. Ensure that your discussions about civil leaders, neighbors, and fellow church members are seasoned with grace, truthful speech, and prayers for their welfare (Colossians 4:6; Jeremiah 29:7), reflecting the peace and righteousness of Christ's eternal kingdom.

question: What is the International Christian Church (ICC), and what do they believe?
answer:
The International Christian Church (ICC), also known as the SoldOut Discipleship Movement, is a high-demand, restorationist religious movement founded in 2006 by Kip McKean. It arose as a breakaway faction from the International Churches of Christ (ICOC), which McKean had also previously led before being removed from leadership.

The ICC traces its historical roots through the Boston Movement and the broader Stone-Campbell Restoration tradition, but it operates with a distinct theological and structural framework characterized by authoritarian discipling, exclusive ecclesiology, and a performance-oriented view of salvation.

### Key Beliefs and Distinctives

**1. Sacerdotalism and Conditional Salvation**
The ICC teaches that water baptism by immersion is strictly necessary for the forgiveness of sins and the reception of the Holy Spirit (baptismal regeneration). However, they go beyond traditional Stone-Campbell theology by insisting that a person must first become a fully surrendered "disciple" according to their specific standards before baptism is valid. Consequently, the ICC routinely invalidates baptisms performed in other Christian traditions (and even within other Restoration churches), requiring prospective members to be re-baptized into their movement.

**2. Exclusivism and the True Church**
The ICC generally presents itself as the only true, biblical movement of God on earth today. While individual members may occasionally qualify their language, the formal posture of the movement asserts that true Christians exist almost exclusively within their fellowship, because only they practice their specific definition of radical discipleship and valid baptism. This stands in contrast to the biblical reality that the universal body of Christ consists of all who are united to Jesus by faith across various times and faithful local assemblies (1 Corinthians 1:2; Revelation 7:9-10).

**3. Hierarchical and Authoritarian Discipleship**
A central pillar of the ICC is its mandatory "discipling" structure. Every member is assigned a personal discipler to whom they must confess sins and submit in matters of daily life, including career decisions, dating, finances, personal schedules, and geographic relocation. While Scripture calls believers to mutual accountability, confession, and discipleship (Galatians 6:1-2; James 5:16), it forbids leaders from domineering over the flock of God (1 Peter 5:2-3) and establishes Jesus Christ as the sole mediator between God and man (1 Timothy 2:5).

**4. Performance-Based Assurance and Legalism**
Within the ICC, assurance of salvation is tied heavily to visible performance, particularly evangelistic productivity, mandatory meeting attendance, and financial giving. Members are regularly pressured to meet quotas for inviting strangers to Bible studies. Failure to maintain these expectations is often treated as evidence of unrepentant sin or spiritual falling away, effectively conflating the distinct biblical doctrines of justification (God declaring a sinner righteous solely through faith) and sanctification (the lifelong, Spirit-wrought growth in holiness).

### Biblical Assessment

When evaluated against historic, orthodox biblical Christianity, the teachings of the ICC raise severe doctrinal concerns:

- **The Basis of Justification:** The Bible teaches that salvation is a gift received by grace alone through faith alone in the finished work of Jesus Christ, not by our works, commitment, or ritual performance (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 3:28; Titus 3:5). In the ICC, the Gospel is burdened with human requirements, turning grace into a wage earned through rigorous discipleship.
- **Christian Liberty:** Believers are freed from human legalism to serve Christ with a clear conscience under the guidance of the Holy Spirit and the Word of God (Galatians 5:1; Romans 14:4). The intrusive control exercised by ICC leadership usurps the proper role of the Holy Spirit in the believer's life.

For anyone who has experienced spiritual burnout, manipulation, or confusion through involvement with the ICC, the Gospel offers true rest. Jesus invites the weary not into an exhausting system of human control, but to Himself: "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28).

question: Do some Christmas traditions have pagan origins?
answer:
Some popular Christmas customs—such as bringing evergreen greenery into homes, winter gift-giving, and celebrating near the winter solstice—do have historical connections to ancient European and Roman cultural festivals like Saturnalia, Yule, and Sol Invictus. In the early centuries of the church, Christians frequently sought to redeem the cultural calendar, replacing pagan festivities with celebrations honoring the incarnation of Jesus Christ, the true "Light of the World" (John 8:12). 

Whether a Christian should participate in traditional Christmas customs is a tertiary matter of Christian liberty and conscience, rather than an essential doctrine of salvation. Sincere believers studying the same Scriptures have historically arrived at different conclusions:

* **The View of Christian Liberty and Redemptive Celebration:** Many Christians believe that cultural forms can be sanctified and repurposed to glorify God. Under this view, an evergreen tree serves as a picture of eternal life, lights point to Christ driving out darkness, and gift-giving reflects God's supreme grace in sending His Son. The apostle Paul taught that "the earth is the Lord’s, and everything in it" (1 Corinthians 10:26), meaning practices that once had pagan associations in antiquity carry no inherent spiritual power or pagan meaning when engaged in with a clear conscience toward Christ.
* **The View of Caution and Abstinence:** Other faithful believers, including the historic English Puritans and some contemporary Christians, choose to abstain from certain traditions or avoid celebrating the holiday altogether. This perspective emphasizes avoiding any practice with historical roots in false worship, drawing from biblical warnings against adopting the religious customs of surrounding nations (Deuteronomy 12:30–32). For these Christians, keeping worship strictly bounded by explicit New Testament commands offers greater peace of conscience.

Scripture gives clear guidance on how believers should handle such differences in Romans 14:5–6: "One person regards one day above another, while another regards every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. He who observes a day does so to the Lord." 

If you choose to celebrate Christmas with traditions like trees, carols, and gift-giving, let your heart be directed toward worshiping the Savior who came in the flesh to redeem sinners. If your conscience leads you to refrain, do so in devotion to the Lord, without judging those who celebrate in freedom. In all things, believers are called to maintain charity, keeping the person and work of Jesus Christ at the center of our lives.

question: Where does the Old Testament predict the coming of Christ?
answer:
The Old Testament anticipates the coming of Jesus Christ across its entirety, unfolding God's single plan of redemption through direct prophecies, covenant promises, and historical types (Luke 24:27; Luke 24:44). From its earliest pages to its closing books, the Hebrew Scriptures weave a detailed portrait of the Messiah's lineage, birth, mission, suffering, and ultimate reign.

Several key passages clearly predict the coming of Christ:

**1. The First Promise of a Deliverer (*Protoevangelium*)**
Immediately after the Fall, God promises that the seed of the woman would ultimately crush the head of the serpent, even while suffering a bruised heel (Genesis 3:15). This foundational promise marks the first announcement of the Gospel, pointing ahead to Christ's victory over Satan at the cross (Hebrews 2:14; Romans 16:20).

**2. His Lineage and Kingdom**
God progressively narrowed the family line through which the Messiah would come:
*   **Through Abraham:** God promised Abraham that through his offspring, all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3; Genesis 22:18; Galatians 3:16).
*   **Through Judah:** The royal scepter was promised to the tribe of Judah until the coming of the one to whom it belongs (Genesis 49:10).
*   **Through David:** God made an eternal covenant with David, promising an heir whose throne and kingdom would endure forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 89:3–4; Isaiah 9:6–7; Luke 1:32–33).

**3. The Place and Manner of His Birth**
*   **Born of a Virgin:** Isaiah prophesied that the Lord would give a sign: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel," meaning "God with us" (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:22–23).
*   **Born in Bethlehem:** The prophet Micah identified the humble village where the eternal Ruler would enter history: "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah... out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient times" (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:5–6).

**4. His Substitutionary Suffering and Death**
The most vivid portrait of Christ's saving work appears in the Prophets and Psalms:
*   **The Suffering Servant:** Isaiah describes the Messiah bearing the penalty for our transgressions in clear terms of penal substitution: "He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5; 1 Peter 2:24). Isaiah also predicted His silent submission (Isaiah 53:7), His burial with the rich (Isaiah 53:9), and His offering as a guilt sacrifice (Isaiah 53:10).
*   **The Crucifixion Foreshadowed:** David depicted the agony of crucifixion centuries before the Romans invented it as an execution method, writing of pierced hands and feet, public mocking, and the casting of lots for garments (Psalm 22:1–18; John 19:23–24).

**5. His Resurrection and Eternal Reign**
*   **Resurrection:** David declared that God would not abandon His Holy One to Sheol or allow Him to undergo bodily decay (Psalm 16:10; Acts 2:27–31).
*   **Eternal Priest-King:** Psalm 110:1–4 reveals that David's Lord is seated at the right hand of God, serving as an eternal priest in the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 5:6; Hebrews 7:17).

As you read the Old Testament Scriptures, remember that they are not merely a collection of moral lessons or ancient histories, but a unified narrative designed to build expectation for Jesus Christ, in whom all of God's promises find their fulfillment (2 Corinthians 1:20).

question: What is spiritual adultery?
answer:
Spiritual adultery is the covenant unfaithfulness of God’s people when they give their ultimate love, worship, trust, or loyalty to idols and worldly desires rather than to God Himself. Because God establishes a sacred covenant with His people that is likened to a marriage, turning away from Him to serve other gods or cherish the world is treated in Scripture not merely as a legal violation, but as personal, relational betrayal.

### The Old Testament Background: Israel as the Unfaithful Bride
Throughout the Old Testament, the Lord revealed Himself as the covenant husband of Israel (Isaiah 54:5; Jeremiah 31:32). When Israel turned to the false gods of the surrounding nations or placed their trust in pagan military alliances instead of the living God, the prophets repeatedly condemned this idolatry as marital infidelity. 

The Hebrew Scriptures frequently use the term *zanah* (to commit fornication or play the harlot) to describe this spiritual apostasy (Exodus 34:15-16; Jeremiah 3:6-9; Ezekiel 16:15-32). The prophet Hosea was even commanded by God to marry an unfaithful woman named Gomer as a living portrait of Israel’s persistent unfaithfulness to the Lord, juxtaposed against God’s unwavering, redeeming covenant love (Hosea 1:2; Hosea 3:1).

### The New Testament Context: Worldliness and Divided Affections
In the New Testament, this imagery deepens. The church is revealed as the pure bride of Christ, betrothed to one husband (2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25-32; Revelation 19:7-8). Spiritual adultery occurs whenever believers compromise their devotion to Jesus Christ by conforming to the corrupt desires, values, and systems of the fallen world.

The Apostle James uses this exact language to rebuke believers whose hearts were compromised by worldly ambitions and selfish desires:
> "You adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Therefore, whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God" (James 4:4).

Spiritual adultery in the Christian life is rarely a formal rejection of God; instead, it usually begins as a divided heart. It happens when functional idols—such as wealth, career advancement, human approval, sexual immorality, or comfort—usurp Christ’s rightful place on the throne of our affections (1 John 2:15-17; Colossians 3:5).

### Pastoral Application and the Hope of the Gospel
To guard against spiritual adultery, a concrete step in daily sanctification is to practice regular, prayerful heart examination:
1. **Identify Functional Idols:** Ask yourself honestly where your mind drifts when unoccupied, what you rely on for security, or what you turn to first for comfort during distress.
2. **Repent and Reorient:** Where you find divided loyalty, confess it to the Lord without excuse, asking Him to renew your first love for Christ (Revelation 2:4-5).
3. **Rest in God's Faithfulness:** The glorious message of the Gospel is that while we are prone to wander, Christ gave His life to cleanse and redeem His bride (Titus 2:14). Even when we struggle, "if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself" (2 Timothy 2:13).

question: How can we rely on the power of God?
answer:
We rely on the power of God by acknowledging our own natural weakness, trusting wholly in Christ's sufficiency, and actively yielding to the Holy Spirit through the means of grace He has given us. Biblical dependence is not passive resignation, but an active, daily leaning upon the Lord in faith, obedience, and prayer.

Scripture teaches that the starting point of experiencing God's strength is recognizing our utter inability to save or sanctify ourselves. Jesus stated plainly in John 15:5, "I am the vine; you are the branches. The one who remains in Me and I in him will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing." When the Apostle Paul pleaded for his thorn in the flesh to be removed, the Lord answered him in 2 Corinthians 12:9, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness." True reliance begins when we stop trusting in human resolve and cast ourselves upon the sovereign strength of our Creator.

In practical Christian living, we lay hold of God's power through several foundational rhythms:

1. **Feeding on God's Word:** Faith is fed and strengthened by truth. In Ephesians 6:17, Scripture is called "the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God." When we read, study, and memorize Scripture, the Holy Spirit aligns our minds with God's will and fortifies our hearts against temptation and fear (Romans 10:17; Psalm 119:11).

2. **Communing in Persistent Prayer:** Prayer is the purest expression of reliance upon God. To pray is to declare, "Lord, I need You." Instead of carrying burdens alone, Scripture invites us in Philippians 4:6-7 to bring every need to God with thanksgiving. Take time each day to pray directly to God, asking Him for the strength, wisdom, and self-control that only His Spirit can provide (James 1:5; Galatians 5:22-23).

3. **Resting in the Local Church:** God never intended believers to walk in isolation. He distributes spiritual gifts and supplies encouragement through the fellowship of the saints, the preaching of the Word, and the ordinances (Hebrews 10:24-25; 1 Corinthians 12:12-27). Seeking counsel, accountability, and prayer from mature brothers and sisters in Christ is a tangible way we lean on the strength God provides to His body.

4. **Walking in Faithful Obedience:** Relying on God does not mean doing nothing; it means acting in faith that He will supply the grace as we obey. As Paul writes in Philippians 2:12-13, we "work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose."

As a concrete next step, choose one specific burden or decision you are currently facing, open your Bible to Proverbs 3:5-6, and take five uninterrupted minutes to bring that matter directly to God in prayer, consciously surrendering your own understanding into His capable hands.

In what particular area of your life right now are you finding it most challenging to let go of self-reliance and rest in God's strength?

question: What does it mean that Jesus fulfilled the law, but did not abolish it?
answer:
In Matthew 5:17, Jesus declared, "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them." To say that Jesus fulfilled the Law rather than abolishing it means He brought the entire Old Testament revelation to its intended goal, perfect realization, and ultimate completion.

In the original Greek of the New Testament, the word translated as "fulfill" is *plēroō*, which means to fill full, bring to completion, or accomplish. In the context of Second Temple Judaism, rabbinic debates often focused on how properly to interpret and preserve the Torah. Jesus clarified that His mission was not to set aside God's holy commandments or treat them as obsolete errors, but to realize everything the Law demanded, promised, and anticipated.

Christ fulfilled the Law in several distinct and interconnected ways:

1. **Prophetic and Typological Fulfillment:** The Old Testament sacrificial system, priesthood, and temple pointed forward as shadows to the substance found in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1). As the true Lamb of God, Jesus offered the final, sufficient sacrifice for sins, bringing the ceremonial requirements to their designed end (Hebrews 9:11–14).

2. **Perfect Obedience (His Active Obedience):** God's moral law requires absolute perfection (Leviticus 19:2; Matthew 5:48). Where humanity failed, Jesus lived a sinless life, keeping every command in thought, word, and deed (Galatians 4:4–5; Hebrews 4:15). In doing so, He established the perfect righteousness that is credited to believers through justification by faith alone.

3. **Bearing the Penalty (His Passive Obedience):** The Law pronounces a curse upon everyone who fails to keep all things written in it (Deuteronomy 27:26; Galatians 3:10). On the cross, through penal substitution, Jesus bore the holy wrath of God and paid the penalty for our transgressions, redeeming us from the curse of the Law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

4. **Deepening the True Meaning of the Law:** Throughout the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus revealed the heart of the moral law, demonstrating that God requires inward holiness, not merely external conformity (Matthew 5:21–48). 

Because Christ fulfilled the Law, believers are freed from the Law as a covenant of works for earning salvation (Romans 6:14; Romans 8:1–4). Instead, the Holy Spirit writes God's moral law on our hearts, enabling us to walk in joyful obedience not to achieve righteousness, but out of love for the Savior who secured it for us (Jeremiah 31:33; Romans 13:8–10). 

As a concrete step of reflection this week, read through Romans 8:1–4 in your personal devotions, taking time to thank the Lord that your acceptance before God rests entirely upon Christ's finished obedience and sacrifice on your behalf.

question: What are the Major Prophets and Minor Prophets?
answer:
The distinction between the Major Prophets and the Minor Prophets in the Old Testament refers strictly to the length of the books, not to their spiritual importance or divine authority. Every book in both groups is the inspired, inerrant Word of God, carrying equal weight in revealing His character and redemptive plan.

### The Major Prophets
The Major Prophets comprise five longer books written by four prophets:

* **Isaiah:** Often called the "evangelical prophet," this book contains profound visions of God's holiness, warnings of judgment, and vivid prophecies of the suffering Messiah and His eternal kingdom (Isaiah 6:1-8; Isaiah 53:1-12).
* **Jeremiah:** Known as the "weeping prophet," Jeremiah ministered leading up to and during the fall of Jerusalem, calling the nation to repentance and foretelling the New Covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34).
* **Lamentations:** A collection of five poetic laments over the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, which also highlights God's enduring mercies (Lamentations 3:22-23).
* **Ezekiel:** Written during the Babylonian exile, this book is filled with dramatic apocalyptic visions, emphasizing God's sovereignty, the departure and return of His glory, and the promise of a new heart and Spirit for His people (Ezekiel 36:26-27).
* **Daniel:** Set in the courts of Babylon and Persia, Daniel blends historical narrative with visions of earthly empires and the everlasting kingdom of the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13-14).

### The Minor Prophets
The Minor Prophets consist of twelve shorter books. In the Hebrew Scriptures, these are collected together onto a single scroll known simply as "The Twelve" (*Tere Asar*).

* **Hosea:** Uses the prophet's tragic marriage to an unfaithful wife as a living picture of God's relentless, redeeming love for idolatrous Israel.
* **Joel:** Warns of the coming "Day of the Lord" using the imagery of a locust plague, while looking forward to the outpouring of the Holy Spirit (Joel 2:28-32).
* **Amos:** A shepherd called to proclaim God's demand for true righteousness and social justice rather than empty religious ritual.
* **Obadiah:** A short prophecy announcing judgment against the nation of Edom for their pride and cruelty toward Israel.
* **Jonah:** The narrative of a reluctant prophet sent to Nineveh, displaying God's mercy extending even to Gentile nations.
* **Micah:** Confronts injustice and corruption among leaders and famously foretells the birthplace of the Messiah in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2).
* **Nahum:** Declares God's righteous judgment and the eventual destruction of Nineveh, the capital of the cruel Assyrian empire.
* **Habakkuk:** A dialogue between the prophet and God regarding why the wicked prosper, concluding with the great truth that "the righteous shall live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4).
* **Zephaniah:** Proclaims the approaching Day of the Lord against all nations, while offering the hope of a humble remnant whom God rejoices over with singing (Zephaniah 3:17).
* **Haggai:** Encourages the returned Jewish exiles to rebuild the temple of the Lord and prioritize God's house above their own comforts.
* **Zechariah:** Contemporary with Haggai, this book contains rich messianic visions, including the King coming humbly on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9) and the one whom they pierced (Zechariah 12:10).
* **Malachi:** The final Old Testament book, confronting spiritual apathy and pointing ahead to the forerunner who would prepare the way for the Messiah (Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5-6).

### Biblical Significance
Together, the Major and Minor Prophets served as God's covenant prosecutors, calling Israel and Judah back from idolatry and sin to sincere faith. Crucially, their writings consistently point forward to the coming of Jesus Christ, who fulfilled the righteous requirements of the Law and bore the judgment these prophets foresaw, providing redemption for all who trust in Him (Luke 24:27; Acts 3:18).

question: Why believe in Jesus?
answer:
It is completely natural to ask why one person from ancient history should matter for your life today. Many people reasonably wonder whether Jesus was simply a wise moral teacher among many throughout history, or why Christians claim He is the only mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5). 

We believe in Jesus because of who He is, what He has done to rescue us, and how His historical resurrection confirms His claims.

**1. The Reality of Our Need**
The Bible teaches that God is completely holy, righteous, and good (Isaiah 6:3). He created humanity to know Him, but every one of us has fallen short of His standard through sin, living independently of Him and violating His moral law (Romans 3:23). Because God is perfectly just, sin brings real separation from Him and eternal judgment (Romans 6:23). No amount of good deeds, religious rituals, or self-improvement can erase our guilt or bridge this infinite divide (Ephesians 2:8-9).

**2. The Uniqueness of Christ’s Identity and Life**
Jesus is not merely a good human example; He is God incarnate, truly God and truly man in one person (Colossians 2:9; John 1:1; John 1:14). He came into the world through the virgin birth, lived a life of absolute moral perfection, and fulfilled dozens of specific Old Testament prophecies written centuries before His birth. Where we failed, He perfectly obeyed God's law.

**3. His Atoning Death and Bodily Resurrection**
The heart of the Christian message is what Jesus accomplished on the cross. Out of pure love and mercy, Christ offered Himself as a penal substitutionary sacrifice, taking upon Himself the punishment our sins deserved so that God's justice was satisfied and His grace freely poured out (Romans 5:8; 2 Corinthians 5:21). 

Jesus did not stay in the tomb. On the third day, He rose bodily from the dead, as witnessed by hundreds of people (1 Corinthians 15:3-8). His resurrection proved His divinity, broke the power of death, and validated everything He claimed about Himself (Romans 1:4). He is now exalted as the living Lord over all creation.

**4. The Free Gift of Eternal Life**
Through Jesus alone, God offers full pardon for every sin, true peace of conscience, and the certainty of eternal life (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). This salvation cannot be earned by our works; it is received solely as a gift of grace through faith.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. 

What thoughts or questions come to mind as you consider who Jesus is and what He did?

question: What is a Bible Baptist Church, and what do Bible Baptists believe?
answer:
A Bible Baptist Church is typically an independent, conservative congregation rooted in the historic Baptist tradition, emphasizing the supreme authority of the Scriptures (*sola Scriptura*) and salvation through personal faith in Jesus Christ. Many congregations bearing this name belong to the Independent Baptist movement or are affiliated with fellowships such as the Baptist Bible Fellowship International (BBFI), maintaining complete autonomy from any central denominational hierarchy.

While individual congregations may vary in specific practices or ministry culture, Bible Baptists share a common set of foundational convictions rooted in Scripture:

### 1. The Authority and Inerrancy of Scripture
Bible Baptists affirm that the sixty-six books of the Old and New Testaments are the verbally inspired, infallible, and inerrant Word of God (2 Timothy 3:16-17; 2 Peter 1:20-21). Scripture serves as the final and sufficient authority in all matters of faith, doctrine, and daily Christian practice. Many Bible Baptist churches place a strong emphasis on biblical preservation, with some using the King James Version exclusively in preaching and teaching, while others utilize various reliable modern translations.

### 2. The Nature of God and the Person of Christ
They hold to orthodox Christian theism: one God eternally existing in three co-equal persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14). They affirm the deity and humanity of Jesus Christ, His virgin birth, sinless life, miracles, bodily resurrection from the dead, and personal, visible return in glory (John 1:1; John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Titus 2:13).

### 3. Salvation by Grace Alone Through Faith Alone
Bible Baptists teach that all human beings are born with a fallen, sinful nature and are separated from a holy God (Romans 3:23; Romans 5:12). Salvation is accomplished solely through the penal substitutionary atonement of Jesus Christ, who bore the penalty for sin upon the cross (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). Justification is received as a free gift of God's grace through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ alone, completely apart from human works, rituals, or sacramental merit (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 10:9-10). Most Bible Baptists also affirm the eternal security of the believer, holding that those genuinely born again are kept by God's power (John 10:28-29; Romans 8:38-39).

### 4. Believer’s Baptism and the Ordinances
Following historic Baptist distinctives, Bible Baptists practice two ordinances instituted by Christ, viewing them as symbolic memorials rather than means of saving grace:
*   **Believer’s Baptism (Credobaptism):** Administered exclusively to those who have made a credible profession of faith, performed by full immersion in water as an outward picture of the believer's union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection (Matthew 28:19; Acts 8:36-38; Romans 6:3-4).
*   **The Lord’s Supper:** Observed regularly in remembrance of Christ’s broken body and shed blood on the cross until He returns (1 Corinthians 11:23-26).

### 5. Local Church Autonomy and the Priesthood of All Believers
Bible Baptists operate under an autonomous, congregational form of church government under the singular headship of Jesus Christ (Colossians 1:18). Each local church manages its own internal affairs, property, and missionary support without external governing boards or synods. They recognize two biblical church offices: pastors (also called elders or bishops) and deacons (1 Timothy 3:1-13; Titus 1:5-9). Furthermore, they affirm the priesthood of all believers, meaning every Christian has direct access to God through Christ without need for a human mediator (1 Timothy 2:5; 1 Peter 2:9).

### 6. Personal Holiness and Separation
Many Bible Baptist churches emphasize personal sanctification and separation from worldly practices and false teaching (2 Corinthians 6:14-18; 1 John 2:15-17). This often translates into conservative standards for worship music, lifestyle, and intentional avoidance of ecumenical cooperation with groups that deny foundational Christian truths.

### 7. Eschatology (End Times)
The majority of Bible Baptist churches hold to a dispensational, premillennial understanding of future events. This view anticipates the imminent return of Christ to rapture the Church, followed by a period of tribulation on the earth, the physical return of Christ to establish a literal millennial kingdom, and the final judgment leading to the eternal state (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17; Revelation 20:1-6).

If you are considering visiting or joining a specific Bible Baptist congregation, requesting their written confession of faith or speaking directly with the pastoral leadership will give you clear insight into how that specific local assembly teaches and applies these biblical truths.

question: What is sexual ethics?
answer:
Sexual ethics is the study and application of moral principles regarding human sexuality, addressing its nature, purpose, and proper boundaries. From a Christian perspective, sexual ethics is not an arbitrary list of prohibitions, but is rooted directly in the character of a holy God and His good design for creation (Genesis 1:27; Genesis 2:24).

Scripture teaches that God created sexuality as a good gift designed for intimacy, procreation, and mutual joy, reserved exclusively within the lifelong covenant of marriage between one man and one woman (Hebrews 13:4; Proverbs 5:18-19). In the ancient Greco-Roman world, where sexual exploitation and promiscuity were commonplace, the New Testament established a distinct standard. The biblical writers frequently used the comprehensive term *porneia* (sexual immorality) to identify any sexual activity outside the covenant of marriage as contrary to God's will (1 Thessalonians 4:3-5; 1 Corinthians 6:18). 

Theologically, Christian sexual ethics is directly tied to the doctrine of progressive *sanctification*. Because a believer has been bought with a price through the redemption of Christ, the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and belongs to the Lord (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Furthermore, marital union serves as a profound earthly picture of the sacred, self-giving covenant between Christ and His church (Ephesians 5:31-32). 

Practically, living out biblical sexual ethics requires actively guarding one's mind and habits (Matthew 5:28), honoring God through celibacy in singleness or covenant faithfulness in marriage, and relying upon the Holy Spirit to walk in purity and self-control.

question: What is spiritual sickness? What does it mean to be spiritually sick?
answer:
Spiritual sickness is the state of soul-corruption, moral alienation from God, and inner decay caused by sin. In Scripture, sickness is frequently used as a vivid metaphor for humanity's deep spiritual ruin, where the human heart, blinded by sin and cut off from the life of God, is unable to heal itself.

In the Bible, spiritual sickness is understood in two primary ways:

### 1. The Universal Condition of the Unregenerate (Sin as a Fatal Disease)
At its root, every person outside of Jesus Christ suffers from a fatal spiritual disease inherited from the Fall of mankind, often described in theology as original sin or total depravity. The prophet Isaiah describes this pervasive condition: "The whole head is sick, and the whole heart is faint. From the sole of the foot even to the head, there is no soundness in it, but bruises and sores and raw wounds" (Isaiah 1:5-6). 

Jesus directly applied the metaphor of illness to humanity's need for salvation when He declared, "It is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick. But go and learn what this means: 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice.' For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners" (Matthew 9:12-13). To be spiritually sick in this ultimate sense means being spiritually dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1), utterly unable to cure oneself through moral effort or good works, and in desperate need of regeneration by the Holy Spirit.

### 2. The Believer's Spiritual Decline (Languishing and Backsliding)
For those who are already born again in Christ, spiritual sickness refers to a state of spiritual lethargy, unconfessed sin, compromise with the world, or the neglect of God's grace. Just as physical malnutrition or disease weakens the body, spiritual neglect weakens the soul.

Signs of this spiritual languishing include:
* **A dulled conscience and harboring unconfessed sin:** David described the physical and emotional misery of unconfessed sin, saying, "When I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long" (Psalm 32:3).
* **Loss of love for Christ:** The church in Ephesus worked hard, yet Christ warned them that they had abandoned the love they had at first (Revelation 2:4).
* **Apathy toward the Word of God and prayer:** When spiritual appetite fades, a believer stops hungering for the truth of Scripture (1 Peter 2:2).
* **Hardness of heart and isolation:** Drifting away from Christian fellowship and accountability leaves a believer vulnerable to the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13).

### The Remedy: The Great Physician
Spiritual sickness cannot be resolved by self-help, human philosophy, or religious rituals. The only cure is found in Jesus Christ, who bore our sins upon the cross so that we might be reconciled to God. By His wounds, we are spiritually healed (Isaiah 53:5; 1 Peter 2:24).

If you sense spiritual weariness, distance from God, or a lingering sickness in your soul today:
1. **Examine your heart before God:** Ask the Lord to search you and point out anything that hinders your walk with Him (Psalm 139:23-24).
2. **Confess openly:** Bring every known sin directly to God in prayer, resting on His promise: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).
3. **Return to the means of grace:** Restore a steady daily rhythm of reading God's Word, talking honestly with Him in prayer, and walking closely with a faithful local church where you can be encouraged and strengthened by fellow believers.

question: What is fellowship with God?
answer:
Fellowship with God is the intimate, relational communion and shared life that a believer enjoys with the Triune God, established through the reconciling work of Jesus Christ. In the New Testament, this relationship is captured by the Greek word *koinonia*, which conveys a deep partnership, mutual sharing, and living bond rather than a distant or casual acquaintance (1 John 1:3).

This communion is rooted in what theologians call union with Christ. By nature, our sin alienated us from a holy God, making true relationship impossible on our own merits (Isaiah 59:2; Ephesians 2:12-13). But through the Gospel, Jesus Christ lived a sinless life, died a substitutionary death on the cross to pay the penalty for our sins, and rose bodily from the grave. When a person turns from sin in repentance and trusts in Christ alone, they are justified (declared righteous) and adopted into God's family (Romans 5:1; John 1:12). 

Fellowship with God involves distinct aspects of Christian life:

*   **Communion with the Trinity:** Believers have access to the Father, through the Son, by the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 2:18; 2 Corinthians 13:14). It is a personal reality where God knows you fully, loves you steadfastly, and invites you to know Him.
*   **Walking in the Light:** True fellowship transforms how we live. The Apostle John writes that "if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7). It requires ongoing honesty about our sin, regular confession, and progressive sanctification.
*   **A Two-Way Relationship through the Means of Grace:** God speaks to us authoritatively and tenderly through His inspired Word, the Bible, and we speak to Him in praise, petition, and thanksgiving through prayer.

While our legal standing as God's children is secure in Christ, our daily *experience* of fellowship can be hindered by unconfessed sin, neglect of prayer, or worldly distractions (Psalm 66:18). 

As a concrete step to cultivate this fellowship today, consider establishing a simple daily rhythm: spend fifteen minutes opening God's Word (such as reading a chapter of 1 John or the Psalms), meditating on His character, and speaking honestly to Him in prayer about your needs, sins to confess, and gratitude for His grace.

Are you asking out of a desire to deepen your current walk with the Lord, or are you exploring how to begin a relationship with Him for the first time?

question: What role does Iran play in the end times?
answer:
In biblical prophecy, the geographic territory of modern-day Iran is identified historically as Persia, which appears prominently in Ezekiel 38:5 as one of the allied nations gathered under "Gog, of the land of Magog" in the latter days. 

The precise role that modern Iran plays in the end times is a tertiary matter of eschatology where faithful, Bible-believing Christians hold differing views based on how they interpret prophetic and apocalyptic literature.

**1. The Futurist and Dispensational View**
Many Christians interpret Ezekiel 38–39 as a literal, future military conflict (often called the War of Gog and Magog) that takes place either before or during the end-times tribulation period. In this understanding, because Persia is explicitly listed alongside Cush, Put, Gomer, and Beth-togarmah (Ezekiel 38:5-6), modern Iran will form an active military alliance with northern and Middle Eastern nations to attack the restored nation of Israel. Proponents of this view point to current geopolitical alignments and hostilities in the region as potential precursors to this event, which concludes with God intervening supernaturally to judge the invading armies and reveal His holy name to the nations (Ezekiel 38:21-23).

**2. The Symbolic and Typological View (Historic / Amillennial / Idealist)**
Other faithful Christians understand the prophetic language in Ezekiel 38–39 typologically rather than as a modern geopolitical forecast. In this view, the ancient enemies of Israel (such as Persia, Magog, and Meshech) are used by the prophet as archetypes of worldly, anti-God powers that persecute God's covenant people throughout history. The Apostle John uses this same imagery in Revelation 20:7-9 to describe the final, global gathering of the nations against Christ and His Church immediately prior to the Last Judgment. Rather than predicting specific 21st-century military movements by modern nation-states, these passages are seen as a comforting assurance that all earthly powers opposed to God will ultimately be defeated by King Jesus at His final return.

**3. The Historical-Fulfillment View**
Some scholars emphasize that Ezekiel's prophecies had a primary or initial fulfillment in the historical struggles of post-exilic Israel (such as during the Persian and Hellenistic periods), while establishing the enduring theological principle that God preserves His people against seemingly overwhelming regional powers.

Because Scripture does not explicitly mention the modern political state of Iran by name, believers should exercise humility and avoid dogmatism when mapping contemporary news events onto biblical prophecy. What remains absolute across all orthodox Christian views is that the Lord God is completely sovereign over every earthly ruler and empire (Psalm 2:1-4; Proverbs 21:1). 

Rather than living in anxiety over geopolitical tensions, believers are called to pray for the peace of all nations, support the flourishing of the underground Christian church currently growing rapidly inside Iran, and rest securely in the promise of Christ's return (Matthew 24:6; Philippians 4:6-7).

question: What does Jesus mean when He says, “Verily, verily” or “Truly, truly,” in the gospels?
answer:
When Jesus says “Truly, truly” (or “Verily, verily” in older translations), He is issuing a solemn, authoritative preface to emphasize that the statement following is absolute, divine truth requiring our utmost attention. 

Linguistically, the underlying word in the Greek text is *amēn* (ἀμήν), transliterated directly from the Hebrew and Aramaic word *amen*, which denotes certainty, faithfulness, and truth, often translated as “so be it” or “let it be established.”

In ancient Jewish practice and Old Testament tradition, people used *amen* at the end of a prayer, covenant, or proclamation to affirm agreement with what was said (Deuteronomy 27:15–26; Nehemiah 8:6). Jesus, however, did something unprecedented: He placed *amen* at the very beginning of His sentences. By prefacing His teachings with “Truly, I say to you,” or the doubled “Truly, truly, I say to you” (a hallmark of the Gospel of John, appearing twenty-five times), Jesus was not merely agreeing with someone else's statement. He was introducing His own words with supreme, unshakeable certainty.

This usage carries profound theological significance:

1. **Divine Authority:** Old Testament prophets introduced their messages with “Thus says the Lord,” acknowledging that their authority was derived from God. Jesus, by contrast, declared, “Truly, truly, *I* say to you” (John 3:3; John 5:24). This formula underscores His divine identity; as the incarnate Word of God, He speaks with inherent, divine authority. In Revelation 3:14, Jesus is even given the title “the Amen, the faithful and true witness.”
2. **Solemn Weight and Certainty:** In Hebrew thought, repetition signifies solemnity, intensity, and absolute certainty (similar to how God is declared “Holy, holy, holy” in Isaiah 6:3). When Jesus repeats the word, He signals to His listeners that what follows is vital to eternal life and cannot be ignored.
3. **Core Revelations of the Gospel:** Jesus frequently used this phrase to introduce foundational truths about salvation, eternal life, and His own mission, such as the necessity of the new birth (John 3:3), the gift of eternal life through faith (John 5:24; John 6:47), and His eternal preexistence (John 8:58).

Whenever you encounter “Truly, truly” in your Scripture reading, pause and treat it as a divine signal to listen with reverence. It is a practical reminder to anchor your faith firmly in Christ’s infallible words, knowing that what He promises and commands will stand forever.

question: What should we learn from the tribe of Asher?
answer:
The tribe of Asher teaches us about God’s abundant earthly and spiritual provision, the grave danger of becoming comfortable and passive in our spiritual duties, and the beauty of God’s grace in preserving a humble, faithful remnant.

Asher was the eighth son of Jacob, born to Leah’s servant Zilpah, and his name in Hebrew (*’Asher*) means "happy" or "blessed" (Genesis 30:12–13). When Jacob blessed his sons, he prophesied that "Asher’s food will be rich; he will provide delicacies fit for a king" (Genesis 49:20). Moses similarly pronounced a blessing of prosperity upon the tribe, declaring, "Most blessed of sons is Asher; let him be favored by his brothers and let him dip his foot in oil" (Deuteronomy 33:24–25). When Israel entered the Promised Land, Asher received a fertile territory along the Mediterranean coast, rich in agriculture and famous for its olive groves (Joshua 19:24–31). 

From the history of Asher across Scripture, we can draw three primary lessons:

### 1. Material Prosperity Can Lead to Spiritual Passivity
While God richly endowed Asher with physical blessings, that abundance became an occasion for compromise. In Judges 1:31–32, Asher failed to drive out the Canaanites dwelling in their allotted land and instead settled peacefully among them. Later, when Deborah and Barak summoned the tribes of Israel to fight against the Canaanite king Jabin, Asher remained idle by the coast, preoccupied with their trade and ease (Judges 5:17). 

This serves as a sobering warning: when God grants comfort and material abundance, our natural tendency is to become complacent. Believers must guard their hearts so that earthly security does not displace wholehearted devotion to God and active partnership with His people.

### 2. God Honors Humility and Repentance
Although the northern kingdom of Israel generally fell into persistent idolatry, Asher is specifically mentioned as demonstrating repentance. When King Hezekiah invited all Israel to return to the Lord and celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem, many in the northern tribes mocked the messengers, but "some men of Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and went to Jerusalem" (2 Chronicles 30:11). 

This reminds us that God always looks upon the contrite heart. Regardless of our family heritage, cultural surroundings, or past failures, God welcomes and restores those who turn to Him in humility.

### 3. God Preserves a Faithful Remnant Centered on Christ
In the New Testament, the tribe of Asher reappears in a profound way through the prophetess Anna (Luke 2:36–38). Despite the dispersal and loss of the northern tribes centuries earlier, God preserved this faithful widow from Asher. She spent decades in prayer and fasting in the temple, and she was among the very first to behold the infant Jesus, giving thanks to God and speaking of the Redeemer to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.

Anna’s life illustrates the doctrine of God's preserving grace: God never forgets His people, and true blessedness is found not merely in fertile fields, but in seeing and trusting Jesus Christ, the promised Savior.

---

### Concrete Application
To apply these lessons today, take time this week to audit your own heart regarding comfort and ease. Consider whether physical blessings have caused you to step back from active service or fellowship in your local church, and ask God in prayer to give you the persistent devotion and joyful expectation seen in Anna.

question: Why does the Bible speak against braided hair?
answer:
The Bible does not condemn braided hair as inherently sinful, but rather addresses the heart attitudes of vanity, pride, and the ostentatious display of wealth (1 Timothy 2:9–10; 1 Peter 3:3–4). The apostles were not forbidding personal grooming, but calling believers to prioritize inner godliness over superficial, worldly prestige.

In the first-century Greco-Roman world, elaborate braided hairstyles were often piled high and interwoven with gold ribbons, pearls, and expensive jewels. These styles required hours of labor by enslaved household servants and served as visible status symbols designed to flaunt extreme wealth and social standing. In the context of the gathered church, such extravagant displays caused division, drew attention away from the worship of God, and tempted believers to judge others by worldly measures of affluence.

The Apostle Paul addressed this dynamic directly, instructing that women should "adorn themselves with proper clothing, modestly and discreetly, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly garments, but rather with good works, as is proper for women making a claim to godliness" (1 Timothy 2:9–10). Similarly, the Apostle Peter urged that a believer’s beauty "should not consist of outward things, like braided hair and the wearing of gold jewelry and fine clothes, but rather the hidden person of the heart, with the imperishable quality of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in the sight of God" (1 Peter 3:3–4). 

These passages use a common biblical idiom of comparison: the emphasis is not on absolute prohibition of every braid or adornment, but on the supreme superiority of inner spiritual character over external decoration. The ongoing work of sanctification produces humility, whereas using one's appearance to signal wealth, seduce, or provoke envy directly contradicts the spirit of the Gospel.

For Christians today, this remains a matter of heart posture and Christian liberty. While styles change across cultures, the timeless principle endures: our appearance should be marked by modesty and discretion, with our primary effort directed toward honoring Christ through love and good works. A helpful personal check before the Lord is to ask whether our choices in clothing and grooming aim to draw admiration to ourselves or reflect a humble heart that seeks to honor Him.

question: What is the difference between a covenant and a contract?
answer:
A contract is a legal, transactional agreement between two or more parties based on mutual self-interest and the exchange of goods or services, whereas a covenant is a sacred, life-binding relational bond established by an oath and characterized by enduring faithfulness. While a contract says, "I will fulfill my part if you fulfill yours," a covenant says, "I give myself to you, regardless of the cost."

Scripture reveals several foundational differences between the two:

**1. Nature and Foundation**
Contracts are built on mutual distrust and protection of self-interest; they exist to limit liability and specify what happens if one party fails. In contrast, a covenant is grounded in mutual commitment and personal relationship. In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word for covenant (*berith*) describes a solemn bond characterized by *hesed*, God’s steadfast, covenantal love (Deuteronomy 7:9). 

**2. How They Are Sealed**
In the Ancient Near Eastern world, contracts were negotiated on tablets, but covenants were often "cut" through a solemn sacrificial ceremony (Genesis 15:17–18). By passing through the severed animals, the covenant-makers invoked a self-maledictory oath, essentially declaring that their very lives were pledged to the promise. In the New Testament, this reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ, who sealed the New Covenant (*diatheke*) not with the blood of animals, but with His own blood shed on the cross (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 9:15).

**3. Terms and Duration**
Contracts are conditional and terminate once the specified obligations are met or when one party breaches the terms. Biblical covenants, such as God's covenant with Abraham or the eternal covenant of grace in Christ, are enduring and founded upon the unchangeable character of God (Hebrews 13:20). Even when human beings are unfaithful, God remains faithful to His covenant promises (2 Timothy 2:13).

**4. Primary Focus**
A contract exchanges property, services, or money ("this is mine, that is yours"). A covenant exchanges persons and loyalty ("I am yours, and you are mine"), as seen in the biblical portrait of marriage (Malachi 2:14) and God's relationship with His people (Jeremiah 31:33).

**Practical Application**
Understanding this distinction transforms how we view our walk with the Lord and our relationships with others. Because God relates to us through a covenant of grace rather than a fragile contract, our salvation rests securely on Christ's finished work rather than our fluctuating performance. In daily life, this calls us to approach our marriages and local church commitments not with the consumer mindset of a contract, but with the sacrificial, self-giving love of a covenant.

question: If Jesus was God, why did He say "No one is good but God alone"?
answer:
When Jesus asked, "Why do you call Me good? No one is good but God alone" (Mark 10:18; Luke 18:19), He was not denying His own divinity or moral perfection; rather, He was challenging the young man to realize the full weight of what he was saying. Jesus was directing the man's gaze to the absolute standard of God's goodness to reveal both who Jesus truly is and the man's desperate need for a Savior.

It is entirely understandable why this verse causes people to pause. At first glance, a reader might wonder if Jesus was separating Himself from God or disclaiming goodness altogether. In Jewish thought, however, God alone was recognized as the absolute source and standard of moral perfection (Psalm 106:1; Psalm 119:68). The rich young ruler had approached Jesus calling Him merely "Good Teacher" (Mark 10:17), treating "goodness" as an achievable human trait and regarding Jesus simply as a respected rabbi. 

Jesus responded with a penetrating question to expose two critical realities:

First, Jesus was confronting the man's superficial view of goodness. The man believed he could inherit eternal life by keeping the commandments through his own efforts (Mark 10:20). By establishing that only God possesses inherent, perfect goodness, Jesus showed that human achievement falls far short of God's holy standard (Romans 3:23). 

Second, Jesus was posing a profound theological dilemma regarding His own identity. In essence, Jesus was asking: *Do you understand what "good" truly means? If only God is truly good, and you recognize that I am good, are you prepared to confess that I am God?* Rather than a denial of deity, the statement functions as a pointer to the hypostatic union: the truth that Jesus is both truly God and truly man. If Jesus were merely a man, He could not be inherently good in the ultimate sense. But because He is the eternal Son of God made flesh (John 1:1, 14), the title belongs to Him by right.

The tragic reality of the rich ruler's story is that he walked away sorrowful because he trusted in his own wealth and moral efforts rather than submitting to the God who stood before him. No human being can attain eternal life through personal goodness, because all of us have sinned and fallen short of God's glory. 

This is why the Gospel is such good news. Jesus Christ, who lived the only perfectly good and sinless life, went to the cross to bear the penalty for our sins in our place. He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily from the grave, conquering sin and death. Salvation is not earned through our flawed attempts at goodness, but is given by God's grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone.

Turn from your own self-reliance, repent of your sins, and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, to receive true forgiveness and eternal life. 

As you consider Jesus' question to the young man, who do you believe Jesus is?

question: What does it mean that God will reveal the hidden things (Daniel 2:22 and 28)?
answer:
In Daniel 2:22 and Daniel 2:28, the declaration that God reveals hidden things means that the sovereign Lord possesses total omniscience and supreme authority over history, making known truths and future events that human wisdom could never discover on its own. While the magicians, enchanters, and astrologers of Babylon were entirely powerless to know King Nebuchadnezzar's dream, the living God unveiled both the dream and its prophetic meaning to Daniel, demonstrating that He alone governs the destiny of nations.

### The Historical and Biblical Context
In the Ancient Near Eastern court of Babylon, monarchs depended heavily on occult specialists and omen-readers to discern the will of their gods. King Nebuchadnezzar tested his advisors by demanding that they tell him both the dream he had forgotten and its interpretation, exposing the utter vanity of pagan divination (Daniel 2:10-11). 

When Daniel was summoned, he carefully deflected all praise from human intellect, declaring, "There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries" (Daniel 2:28). In the original Aramaic text of this chapter, the word used for "mystery" or "secret" (*raz*) refers to matters that belong exclusively to God's divine council and can only be known through special revelation. 

### Key Theological Truths

1. **God's Absolute Omniscience and Sovereignty**
   Daniel 2:22 states that God "reveals deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him." Nothing in creation is concealed from God's sight (Hebrews 4:13; Psalm 139:11-12). He knows not only the secret motives of human hearts, but also the entire course of future history, because He is the sovereign Lord who ordains the rise and fall of earthly kingdoms (Daniel 2:21).

2. **The Unfolding of Redemptive History**
   The specific "hidden thing" revealed in Daniel 2 was God's grand design for the ages: a succession of earthly empires that would eventually be shattered and replaced by an everlasting kingdom established by God Himself (Daniel 2:44-45). In the New Testament, this concept of a revealed "mystery" finds its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ and the Gospel, which was once hidden in types and shadows but is now fully made known to the world (Romans 16:25-26; Ephesians 3:4-6).

3. **The Exposure of Secret Realities at the Final Judgment**
   Scripture also teaches that God revealing the hidden things extends to the final day of judgment. The Lord will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and disclose the motives of men's hearts (Ecclesiastes 12:14; 1 Corinthians 4:5; Romans 2:16). For the unbeliever, this is a sober warning of divine justice, but for those in Christ, it is a reminder that no righteous deed or hidden suffering done for His glory is ever overlooked.

### Pastoral Application
For the Christian today, this truth offers great peace. When your path feels dark, confusing, or uncertain, you can place your confidence in the God who sees through the darkness and holds the future securely. 

A practical way to apply this is to bring the uncertainties of your life before Him in prayer today. Instead of carrying the anxiety of tomorrow, entrust your unseen circumstances and quiet fears to the Father, resting in His sovereign care and perfect wisdom (Matthew 6:31-34; Proverbs 3:5-6).

question: What items should be included in a church constitution?
answer:
A church constitution is a foundational governing document that establishes a local congregation's theological convictions, organizational order, and relational commitments so that all things are done "decently and in order" (1 Corinthians 14:40). While secondary structures of governance vary across faithful traditions (such as elder-led congregationalism or presbyterian oversight), a thorough and biblically grounded constitution generally includes the following essential sections:

### 1. Name and Purpose
This section defines the official legal and ecclesiastical name of the church, along with its biblical mission: to glorify God through the proclamation of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the making of disciples, and faithful worship (Matthew 28:18-20; 1 Corinthians 10:31).

### 2. Statement of Faith
The confession of faith articulates the doctrinal boundaries of the church. It should clearly define non-negotiable core doctrines, including:
* The divine inspiration, inerrancy, and supreme authority of the Bible (2 Timothy 3:16-17; 2 Peter 1:20-21).
* The Trinity (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14).
* The full deity and humanity of Jesus Christ, His virgin birth, sinless life, substitutionary atoning death, bodily resurrection, and physical return (John 1:1, 14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Titus 2:13).
* Justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 3:24-26).
* The church's secondary convictions regarding baptism, the Lord's Supper, and the nature of the covenant community.

### 3. Church Covenant
A church covenant is a solemn, practical pledge where members agree before God to walk together in Christian love, holiness, mutual accountability, regular attendance, and financial stewardship (Hebrews 10:24-25; Ephesians 4:1-3).

### 4. Membership
This section details how individuals enter into and depart from the local body:
* **Qualifications:** A credible profession of repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, obedience in baptism, and agreement with the statement of faith and covenant.
* **Process of Admission:** Pastoral interview, congregational affirmation, and public reception.
* **Termination of Membership:** Voluntary transfer to another gospel-preaching church, death, resignation, or the final step of corrective discipline.

### 5. Church Leadership and Offices
Scripture identifies two ordinary, continuing offices in the local church:
* **Elders / Pastors / Overseers:** Biblical qualifications (1 Timothy 3:1-7; Titus 1:5-9), duties of spiritual oversight, preaching the Word, praying for the flock, and shepherd-care (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:1-4; Hebrews 13:17).
* **Deacons:** Biblical qualifications (1 Timothy 3:8-13) and duties of physical service, mercy ministry, and administrative care, freeing the elders to focus on prayer and the ministry of the Word (Acts 6:1-6).
* **Selection and Removal:** Clear procedures for nominating, examining, electing, ordaining, and, if necessary, biblically removing an officer (1 Timothy 5:19-20).

### 6. The Ordinances (Sacraments)
A statement governing the regular, faithful administration of:
* **Baptism:** The public immersion of a professing believer into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19; Romans 6:3-4).
* **The Lord's Supper:** The commemorative, spiritual communion in Christ's body and blood for baptized believers walking in fellowship with God and His church (1 Corinthians 11:23-29).

### 7. Church Discipline and Restoration
To protect the purity of the church, guard the name of Christ, and reclaim wandering sheep, the constitution must outline the redemptive steps of biblical church discipline as commanded by our Lord (Matthew 18:15-17; 1 Corinthians 5:1-13; Galatians 6:1). This includes private confrontation, pastoral involvement, congregational admonition, and, if unrepentant, removal from fellowship, always with the goal of repentance and restoration.

### 8. Congregational Meetings and Governance
This section defines how church decisions are conducted:
* Frequency of members' meetings (annual, quarterly).
* Matters reserved for congregational vote (e.g., calling pastors, approving the annual budget, admitting or removing members, acquiring real property).
* Quorum requirements and voting thresholds.

### 9. Finances and Property (Dissolution Clause)
Guidelines for handling tithes, offerings, and designated funds with complete integrity (2 Corinthians 8:20-21), as well as a standard legal dissolution clause stipizing that all church assets will be transferred to another tax-exempt, like-minded gospel ministry if the congregation ever dissolves.

### 10. Amendments
The exact procedure, notification timeline, and voting majority required to modify the constitution or bylaws in the future.

***

**Practical Next Step:** If your church is drafting or revising a constitution, begin by reviewing the historical confessions of the church (such as the Second London Baptist Confession of 1689 or the Westminster Confession of Faith) and consult the constitutions of healthy sister congregations to ensure both doctrinal clarity and legal compliance with your local jurisdiction.

question: What is topical preaching? Should a pastor preach topically?
answer:
Topical preaching is a method of sermon preparation and delivery where the preacher begins with a specific subject, doctrine, or question (such as marriage, prayer, suffering, or stewardship) and gathers various passages across Scripture to address that topic. Unlike consecutive verse-by-verse preaching through a single biblical book, the structure of a topical sermon is organized around the theme itself.

Whether a pastor should preach topically is a matter of pastoral wisdom and homiletical method rather than an essential doctrine of the faith. Scripture commands pastors to "preach the word" (2 Timothy 4:2) and to declare "the whole counsel of God" (Acts 20:27), but it does not mandate a single sermon structure.

Historically and practically, faithful Christians hold differing views on the role of topical preaching in the life of the local church:

* **In favor of topical preaching:** Advocates point out that topical preaching enables a pastor to address timely pastoral needs, urgent cultural questions, and specific doctrinal subjects by synthesizing what the whole canon of Scripture teaches on an issue (*systematic theology*). It can be deeply edifying for a congregation to see how a doctrine spans from Genesis to Revelation.
* **Caution regarding topical preaching:** Many pastors prefer consecutive expository preaching as the primary diet of the pulpit. The main argument for this approach is that preaching through books of the Bible ensures that God's Word sets the agenda rather than the pastor's personal preferences, protects the pulpit from proof-texting, and forces the congregation to confront difficult texts that might otherwise be overlooked.

A balanced and widely practiced approach is to make consecutive verse-by-verse expository preaching the main diet of the congregation, while occasionally utilizing topical series or standalone sermons to address specific doctrinal, ethical, or pastoral needs. 

Whatever format is used, the essential requirement is faithful *exegesis*: every Scripture passage cited in a topical sermon must be handled accurately within its original historical and literary context, pointing believers ultimately to Christ and the authority of His Word. When listening to or preparing a topical message, a helpful practice is to read the surrounding chapter of every cited verse to ensure the text is actually saying what the sermon claims.

question: What are tribulation saints?
answer:
"Tribulation saints" is a theological term referring to believers who place their faith in Jesus Christ during the time of unprecedented global distress and judgment known as the Great Tribulation, described in passages such as Revelation 7:14 and Matthew 24:21. 

Because details regarding the end times are tertiary matters where faithful, Bible-believing Christians hold differing convictions, the specific identification of these saints depends on one's broader eschatological framework.

*   **Dispensational Premillennialism:** In this view, the church is raptured before a literal seven-year tribulation period. Consequently, "tribulation saints" refers specifically to individuals, both Jews and Gentiles, who turn to Christ *after* the church has been caught up to heaven. These believers face fierce persecution under the Antichrist and are often martyred for refusing the mark of the beast, as pictured in Revelation 13:7 and Revelation 20:4.
*   **Historic Premillennialism, Amillennialism, and Postmillennialism:** In these historic perspectives, the church is not removed prior to the tribulation. Instead, the church traverses the trials of this present age, including any climactic final distress, until the bodily return of Christ. From this standpoint, the saints depicted in the book of Revelation (such as the great multitude in Revelation 7:9–14) represent the entire redeemed people of God who endure suffering and remain faithful through the power of the Holy Spirit.

While faithful Christians disagree on the precise prophetic timeline, Scripture provides absolute assurance on the core truth: God sovereignly preserves and sustains His elect through every trial. As Revelation 7:14 declares, those who overcome do so because "they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb." For every believer today, the call is to rest in the finished work of Christ and stand firm in faithful obedience, whatever trials may come.

question: Who are the Black Hebrews / Black Israelites?
answer:
